To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that

(a) a hierarchical model can be used for the analysis of nonrandomly censored ordered categorical longitudinal data from analgesic trials and that (b) this analysis can be used to address the question of what dosing patterns to recommend.
the hierarchical model is more appropriate than a marginal model for addressing the dosing question in a clinical trial of an oral analgesic agent.
the proposed hierarchical model for ordered categorical data with nonrandom right censoring is useful for addressing both questions of a clinical trial of an active agent for pain relief.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the analysis of longitudinal data in which the outcome of interest is an ordered categorical variable.
the development and application of statistical methodology for the analysis of data from clinical trials of analgesic drugs.
the use of hierarchical modeling to analyze longitudinal data in the context of clinical trials.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
the drug relives pain and, based on extrapolation from the data, the drug should be dosed at a rate of 30 mg/hr.
the drug is effective, and that the dosage pattern of interest is 30 mg every 6 hours, with 60 mg as an alternative.
the drug relives pain and that the dosing pattern recommended for further study is 30 mg, followed by 15 mg if pain relief is inadequate.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
a semimechanistically based hierarchical analysis of nonrandomly censored ordered categorical longitudinal data can address both questions in a clinical trial of an active analgesic agent.
the hierarchical approach is useful for the analysis of data from a clinical trial of a new analgesic drug.

the proposed analysis is more credible than a conventional marginal analysis because it is semimechanistic and because it uses subject matter information in extrapolating from the dosing patterns actually observed in the study to the dosing patterns of interest to a typical patient.
The main takeaway from our work is that
a semimechanistically specified model, in contrast to a marginal model, can be used to answer both the proof-of-efficacy and dosing questions in a trial.
the analysis of a trial of a new drug is best done using a model that incorporates both the pharmacology of the drug and the subject matter of the trial, rather than a purely empirical analysis.

the use of subject matter knowledge to guide model specification is essential in the design and analysis of clinical trials of drugs with nonlinear pharmacokinetics. © 2011 American Statistical Association.
